papers.title: mTOR signalling, not clock gene rhythms, organises daily physiology
papers.abstract: Daily rhythms in mammalian physiology are widely attributed to rhythmic transcription of "clock-controlled genes" driven by the circadian transcriptional/translational feedback loop (TTFL). Here we show that daily physiology can be uncoupled from the TTFL: inhibiting the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) abolishes most daily variation in cellular and organismal physiology, whilst clock protein rhythms persist. In cultured cells and mouse liver, functional rhythms are lost, including the proteome, RNA abundance, substrate utilisation and drug metabolism. In forebrain, most daily variation in protein abundance and phosphorylation is lost, yet locomotor activity and sleep-wake architecture are largely preserved in mice and zebrafish. PERIOD2 binds mTORC1 and limits its activity, providing a route by which clock proteins shape daily mTOR signalling. mTOR inhibition preferentially suppresses output over clock gene rhythms in Arabidopsis and Neurospora. We conclude that mTOR is a conserved conduit through which circadian and environmental timing impose daily organisation on physiology.

papers.title: Diphenhydramine disrupts sleep architecture in 5XFAD Alzheimer's disease model and wild-type mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disruption is common in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Diphenhydramine (DPH), a first-generation antihistamine with anticholinergic properties, is widely used as an over-the-counter sleep aid. We tested whether chronic DPH treatment alters sleep architecture in 5XFAD and wild-type female mice. Female 5XFAD (n = 16) and wild-type (WT) littermates (n = 14) were implanted with wireless telemetry recording devices to measure electroencephalography (EEG) and electromyography (EMG) continuously. After a 24h baseline recording at 5 months of age, mice received oral DPH (10 mg/kg) or vehicle at ZT0 for one month. After this chronic treatment, sleep was recorded continuously for 48h during ongoing dosing. Sleep was scored as rapid eye movement (REM), non-rapid eye movement (NREM) 1, NREM2, or wake. A survival curve analysis was used to investigate the microarchitecture of sleep phases after chronic diphenhydramine treatment. At baseline, 5XFAD female mice had more time in NREM1 than WT female controls and had shorter REM and NREM2 bouts. Chronic DPH treatment fragmented NREM2 in both genotypes, reducing long NREM2 bouts. DPH increased total duration of NREM1 and REM during the active phase, and disrupted the light-dark distribution of sleep. DPH did not rescue 5XFAD sleep deficits; instead, DPH treatment resulted in NREM2 fragmentation. Overall, chronic DPH use degrades sleep quality and increases fragmentation in both WT and AD-model female mice, which questions the use of sedating anticholinergics as sleep aids, especially in AD.

papers.title: Characterization of Sleep, Spectral, and Epileptiform Activity in Individuals Aged 8-27 Years with SYNGAP1-Related Disorder Using an at-Home Dry EEG Headband
papers.abstract: SYNGAP1-related disorder (SYNGAP1-RD) is associated with sleep disturbances, seizures, and neurophysiological abnormalities. However, in-lab EEG can be difficult to obtain due to the behavioral and sensory disorders associated with this condition. In this study we collected EEG in SYNGAP1-RD participants (n=30 enrolled, 27 contributing data) in a decentralized protocol using a dry electrode headband as a path to longitudinal, research-grade data collection in this population. At-home data collection was successful with 180 recordings containing over 1 hour of usable data collected from 23 participants. Across these recordings, sporadic interictal epileptiform discharges were present in 22 of 23 participants but electrographic seizures were not observed. Relative to an adolescent control population (n=10), SYNGAP1-RD participants showed increased wake after sleep onset, reduced sleep efficiency, and decreased time in N1 and N3 sleep stages along with increased time in N2. We reproduced prior findings from awake spectral EEG analyses, including elevated broadband power along with reduced relative alpha power and alpha-theta ratio in the SYNGAP1 cohort. Notably, differences in spectral power were tightly linked to sleep stage, revealing sleep-stage-dependent spectral biomarker dynamics not previously characterized in SYNGAP1-RD. Finally, we examined differences between variants producing truncations downstream of the GAP domain and those producing truncations before or within it, but analyses were limited by a small sample size (n=4 for the post-GAP variant). Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of at-home multi-night sleep EEG collection in participants with SYNGAP1-RD and led to both corroborative and novel findings.

papers.title: Sleep neurophysiology as a biological correlate of infant temperament.
papers.abstract: Temperament, characterized as individual differences in reactivity and self-regulation, influences our behavior in everyday situations. It is apparent as early as infancy and shaped by genetic and environmental factors. A neurophysiological marker of temperament has been quantified during the waking state; however, it remains unknown how these associations manifest in sleep. To address this gap, we assessed nighttime sleep in 29 6-month-old infants (Mage = 6.145 months, SD = 0.399, 48% males) using a portable high-density electroencephalography. Temperament was assessed using a parent-rated questionnaire, focusing on 2 scales: negative affectivity and orienting/regulatory capacity. The correlation analyses included: (i) frontal asymmetry and (ii) whole-brain, electrode-wise correlations with temperament. The predefined frontal asymmetry correlation revealed that increased left-hemispheric slow-wave activity (SWA) corresponded to higher orienting/regulatory capacity scores. The whole-brain correlation showed that higher theta power across an array of electrodes over the prefrontal regions was associated with decreased negative affectivity scores. Local sleep depth over frontal and temporal brain areas, as reflected by SWA asymmetry and theta power, serves as a marker of self-regulatory abilities and affective traits, which, in turn, reflect differences in temperament. Our findings reveal that sleep neurophysiology is a biological correlate of temperament during preverbal stages.

papers.title: Measuring Sleep at Home in Adolescents With Autism Using EEG Headbands: Protocol for a Remote Study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are prevalent in autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and worsen daytime functioning, yet their neural bases remain poorly understood. This may reflect the challenges of laboratory-based polysomnography for individuals with ASD, including sensory sensitivities and difficulty adapting to changes in routine. The advent of wearable electroencephalography (EEG) devices allows for remote data collection in the home and facilitates large-scale sleep studies. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that thalamocortical circuit dysfunction contributes to poor sleep in ASD by characterizing sleep oscillations that rely on this circuitry. To achieve this goal, we monitored sleep in the home using wearable EEG headbands in adolescents with ASD, including those who are profoundly affected, and their typically developing peers. When necessary, we used a desensitization protocol to gradually acclimate participants to wearing the headband overnight to promote the inclusion of individuals with sensory sensitivities and high support needs. Participants and their families completed assessments and questionnaires and received remote training to use a wearable EEG headband. Those needing time to acclimate followed a personalized 2-week desensitization protocol with a practice headband. Sleep was monitored at home for 3 consecutive nights, the first of which was for adaptation to the headband. Sleep data quality was checked daily, and remote technical support was provided as needed. Using sleep rhythms as physiological biomarkers of thalamocortical circuit function, we will test the hypothesis that abnormal circuit function in ASD is related to worse sleep quality. This study was funded by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative (SFARI) and approved by the Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board in November 2021. Data were collected between July 2023 and November 2025. A total of 146 participants (ASD: n=77; typically developing [TD]: n=65; profound autism: n=4) completed the study and produced at least 1 night of usable sleep data. Data analysis is underway, and the results will be submitted for publication in November 2026. At-home sleep monitoring enables large samples that are needed to characterize the neural underpinnings of sleep disturbances across the autism spectrum. The personalized desensitization protocol promotes inclusion by accommodating individuals often excluded from research due to sensory or behavioral challenges. These methods are adaptable for other conditions and research goals beyond ASD, such as longitudinal studies across development or characterizing sleep in other neurodevelopmental disorders. Desensitization protocols may also increase the tolerability of diagnostic laboratory-based sleep studies and other medical procedures, improving both patient experience and quality of care.

papers.title: Improved motor learning in adenosine A1 receptor knockout mice.
papers.abstract: Adenosine is a widespread neuromodulator, acting at A1 and A2A receptors in the brain. Adenosine plays role in a multitude of functions including sleep, homeostasis, neuroprotection and synaptic plasticity. Deletion of A1Rs in knock-out mice (A1R KO) revealed non-uniform effects on learning: learning sequential visual discrimination tasks was impaired, while spatial learning (Morris maze) and working memory tasks were not. Motor learning was also preserved in A1R KO mice. However, a systematic comparison of motor learning in KO and wild type (WT) mice has not been performed. Here we fill this knowledge gap by comparing motor learning in WT and A1R KO mice using an accelerating rotarod task. Both genotypes acquired motor skill and retained it after 1 week without further training. Genotype and Age had significant effects on improvement of motor skills relative to initial performance. A1R KO mice showed higher rate of learning than WT across training days, and reached better performance by the end of training (Day 5). However, retention after 1 week was better in WT mice, which improved relative to last day of training, while KO animals performed at the same level. We saw no differences between females and males, but older animals showed greater gains during learning and better retention. Finally, individual variability of motor learning was not related to measures of baseline motor activity, or anxiety. These results add new pieces to a multifaceted and intriguing picture of shifts in the brain functions resulting from A1R loss and warrant further exploration.

papers.title: Motor memory consolidation during sleep after stroke: the rehabilitation timing hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Motor recovery after stroke depends on neuroplasticity-driven reorganisation of surviving cortical circuits. A growing body of evidence implicates sleep as an active consolidator of motor memories acquired during rehabilitation. Yet stroke disrupts the very sleep architecture required for this process, and current clinical practice schedules rehabilitation without regard for its temporal proximity to sleep. This review synthesizes the mechanistic, preclinical, and emerging clinical evidence underlying the rehabilitation timing hypothesis. Sleep spindles, nested within slow oscillations during NREM sleep, are a principal electrophysiological substrate for motor memory consolidation, and emerging evidence implicates cerebellar-cortical dynamics during spindles. Stroke disrupts this oscillatory coupling through lesion-related alterations in thalamocortical circuitry, GABAergic signalling, and interhemispheric synchrony. Preclinical studies demonstrate that optogenetically-enhanced slow waves during sleep accelerate motor recovery, while pharmacological GABA modulation restores consolidation-promoting oscillations. Chronobiological evidence from healthy adults and older populations suggests that evening training followed by nocturnal sleep may produce superior long-term motor retention compared with morning training. The rehabilitation timing hypothesis is plausible and clinically testable, but direct evidence in stroke populations is currently lacking. Scheduling motor therapy close to sleep is a low-cost strategy that warrants formal evaluation as a means of enhancing stroke recovery. Formal clinical trials testing therapy timing as an independent variable are urgently needed.

papers.title: Cross-Domain Slow Wave Sleep Detection from Single-Lead EEG in Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Recovery.
papers.abstract: Slow wave sleep (SWS) is vital for neural recovery and cardiovascular stability in children following congenital heart disease (CHD) surgery. However, pediatric CHD sleep patterns are often disrupted by clinical stressors and exhibit substantial domain discrepancies relative to adult data distributions. To address these challenges, this study establishes the Pediatric Cardiac Post-surgical Sleep (PCPS) dataset, a self-collected and expert-annotated pediatric polysomnography (PSG) dataset specifically targeting the early post-CHD surgical period. We further propose PCPS-SleepNet, an end-to-end deep learning framework for cross-domain sleep staging from single-lead EEG, enabling effective knowledge transfer from public sleep data to pediatric post-surgical CHD data. The architecture employs a multi-band input representation across six sub-bands and leverages a Four-Stage Progressive Encoder integrating Multi-Scale Depthwise Convolution (MSDC) for local features, self-attention for global density modeling, and a Conformer block for hybrid refinement. To mitigate limited pediatric data availability and domain shift, this network is pre-trained on public datasets and fine-tuned on the PCPS dataset. Subject-independent validation showed competitive performance, with an overall accuracy of 75.65 ± 0.58%, an AUROC of 89.06 ± 0.18%, an AUPRC of 83.49 ± 0.13%, and a macro F1-score of 76.68 ± 0.70%. For SWS detection, the model achieved an AUPRC of 87.89 ± 0.20% and an F1-score of 81.55 ± 0.74%. Architectural ablations and frequency-band input contribution analysis supported the model design and suggested the complementary discriminative value of slow-wave frequency-band inputs. These results suggest a practical and patient-friendly sleep detection solution for individualized sleep assessment and rehabilitation in vulnerable pediatric populations.

papers.title: Circadian-melatonin signaling in general anesthesia: molecular mechanisms and perioperative implications.
papers.abstract: Anesthesia and surgery are delivered to a temporally organized organism whose physiology is governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus, peripheral molecular clocks, and pineal melatonin signaling. This review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and clinical evidence on how anesthetic agents, surgical stress, and the perioperative environment interact with circadian and melatonergic signaling, and on whether that interaction can be targeted therapeutically. In rodent and cellular studies, volatile and intravenous anesthetics alter clock function in an agent- and phase-dependent manner; proposed mechanisms include GABAergic and glutamatergic modulation of entrainment, transcriptional and chromatin-level repression of CLOCK-BMAL1/PER-CRY signaling, and metabolic coupling through CaMK-CREB, AMPK, SIRT1, and GSK-3β. These mechanisms have not been confirmed in humans. In patients, these effects are inseparable from surgical injury, opioids, fasting, inflammation, and disrupted light-dark exposure, all of which suppress melatonin amplitude, delay its onset, and promote internal desynchrony. Melatonin signals through MT1 and MT2 receptors to produce chronobiotic, anxiolytic, and antinociceptive effects, whereas the mitochondrial, redox, and anti-inflammatory actions, described almost exclusively in animal and cellular models, require substantially higher exposures and have not been demonstrated in surgical patients; the two arms are pharmacologically distinct and should not be pooled. Clinically, preoperative anxiolysis with melatonin in adults is the most consistently supported indication, whereas evidence for postoperative sleep, analgesia, delirium prevention, and organ protection remains heterogeneous and of low certainty. Most trials have used fixed clock-time dosing without measuring internal circadian phase or achieved plasma exposure, so null results cannot distinguish an ineffective mechanism from an inadequate intervention. The circadian-melatonin axis remains a plausible perioperative target, but clinical translation requires phase-aware, exposure-informed, and adequately powered trials.

papers.title: Sequential Associations of Sleep Architecture, Nocturnal Oxygenation, and Respiratory Disturbance With a Composite PSG-Derived Rhythm-Event Index.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), particularly obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), has been associated with cardiovascular complications including cardiac arrhythmias. However, the relative contributions of respiratory, oxygenation, and sleep architecture indices to composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index remain incompletely understood. To investigate the sequential associations of sleep architecture, nocturnal oxygenation, and respiratory disturbance indices with the composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index in patients undergoing polysomnography (PSG). Demographic, respiratory, oxygenation and sleep-architecture variables were extracted from PSG records. The primary outcome was a composite PSG-derived rhythm-event count, estimated as round(arrhythmia index × TST_hours) from the PSG-exported arrhythmia index, which was calculated during total sleep time only. Negative binomial regression used an offset of log(TST_hours). Because the outcome demonstrated overdispersion, negative binomial regression with an offset of log(TST hours) was used. Because the original 14-predictor model was over-parameterized for the sample size, a six-predictor model (age, sex, BMI, AHI, T90, and sleep efficiency) was chosen post hoc. This reduced model was not prespecified before the original analysis. Sleep efficiency was retained because it showed a strong signal in the exploratory 14-predictor model. The resulting p-values should therefore be interpreted as optimistic and exploratory. A sequential model-building approach (Model 1: age, sex, BMI, AHI; Model 2: plus T90; Model 3: plus sleep efficiency) was used to document the incremental contribution of each domain. A fully adjusted 14-predictor model was fitted only as a supplementary analysis. Wald 95% CIs and bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (2000 resamples) are reported. Forty-one participants were included (mean age 47.8 ± 13.5 years; median BMI 29.4 kg/m2). Severe OSA (AHI ≥ 30 events/hour) was present in 56.1%. Median arrhythmia index was 3.2 events/hour, with marked overdispersion. In the six-predictor model, only higher sleep efficiency was associated with lower arrhythmia rate (IRR = 0.946 per 1 percentage-point increase, 95% CI 0.921-0.972, p < 0.001; bootstrap 95% CI 0.888-0.984). T90 was associated in the Wald inference (IRR = 1.034, 95% CI 1.006-1.063, p = 0.016) but this association was not robust under bootstrap resampling (95% CI 0.979-1.067). AHI was not associated with arrhythmia rate (IRR = 1.000, 95% CI 0.987-1.014, p = 0.954). Age, sex and BMI were also not significant. A 14-predictor exploratory model had a marginally lower AIC (411.4) but a substantially higher BIC (438.8), consistent with overfitting. In this exploratory selected sleep-center cohort, AHI and other respiratory-event indices were not independently associated with the composite PSG-derived rhythm-event index. Only higher sleep efficiency showed a robust association with lower arrhythmia rate, but this finding is hypothesis-generating and may reflect unmeasured confounding. These results require confirmation in larger prospective studies and should not guide clinical risk stratification.

papers.title: Sigma-1 receptor alleviates postoperative cognitive dysfunction exacerbated by preoperative acute sleep deprivation in mice via modulating the Keap1/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
papers.abstract: Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) is a common neurological complication severely affecting patient prognosis. Preoperative acute sleep deprivation, a frequent perioperative stressor, significantly exacerbates POCD severity. Sigma-1 receptor (σ-1R), an endoplasmic reticulum molecular chaperone, plays a crucial role in modulating neuroinflammation and oxidative stress. However, whether σ-1R can serve as an interventional target to mitigate sleep deprivation-aggravated cognitive impairment remains insufficiently elucidated. This study aimed to clarify the regulatory role of σ-1R in a mouse model combining preoperative sleep deprivation with exploratory laparotomy, focusing on Keap1/Nrf2 signaling, and to evaluate its clinical translational potential. Behavioral, molecular biological, and morphological methods were utilized. Sleep deprivation exacerbated postoperative cognitive impairment, accompanied by a compensatory upregulation of σ-1R expression in hippocampal microglia. Notably, exogenous potentiation of σ-1R with the agonist PRE-084 reversed cognitive deficits, suppressed neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, promoted Nrf2 nuclear translocation, and upregulated downstream genes HO-1 and NQO1; conversely, the antagonist BD-1047 worsened the damage. Mechanistically, σ-1R physically associated with Keap1, promoting Nrf2 release. The Nrf2 inhibitor ML385 blocked PRE-084's protective effects. In vitro experiments confirmed PRE-084 alleviated inflammation and oxidative stress via an Nrf2-dependent pathway. Moreover, σ-1R signaling may partially contribute to the neuroprotective effects of dexmedetomidine. In conclusion, this study reveals that σ-1R activation is associated with protective effects in sleep deprivation-exacerbated POCD, potentially through regulating the Keap1/Nrf2 signaling pathway, a mechanism rarely reported in this context, suggesting σ-1R as a potential avenue for further investigation in POCD prevention.

papers.title: A representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework for spectral analysis and detection of epileptiform patterns in pediatric EEG: computational validation with a roadmap for external benchmarking.
papers.abstract: Pediatric EEG analysis for epilepsy detection is challenged by the non-stationary and developmentally heterogeneous nature of epileptiform activity. Conventional Fourier approaches provide limited time-frequency localization, whereas single-domain methods such as the wavelet transform and empirical mode decomposition (EMD) each exhibit complementary weaknesses. We developed a representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion framework that integrates wavelet and EMD spectra before feature extraction. The pipeline included adaptive wavelet denoising, energy-criterion EMD, weighted time-frequency fusion, extraction of eight spectral-temporal features, and classification using a soft-voting ensemble of a radial basis function support vector machine, random forest, and neural network. Evaluation was performed on 2,000 synthetic pediatric EEG segments spanning canonical epileptiform morphologies and multiple signal-to-noise ratios. A feature-level fusion variant was implemented as an ablation comparator to isolate the effect of fusion strategy while preserving identical feature extraction, classifier architecture, and validation procedures. Across 10-fold stratified cross-validation with 100 Monte Carlo replications, the proposed framework achieved 94.6 ± 0.6% accuracy, 93.7 ± 0.8% sensitivity, 95.5 ± 0.5% specificity, F1 score of 0.943 ± 0.007, and AUROC of 0.971 (95% CI, 0.962-0.978). Performance exceeded standalone wavelet, EMD, and Fourier baselines (all p < 0.001). Representation-level fusion also outperformed feature-level fusion by 1.4 percentage points in accuracy, with the greatest gains observed for polyspike and slow-wave morphologies. On the synthetic corpus the framework was competitive with EEGNet and a 1D convolutional network while retaining explicit time-frequency interpretability. In an external feasibility validation on the CHB-MIT pediatric scalp EEG corpus (14 subjects, leave-one-subject-out), representation-level fusion attained the highest performance of all methods (AUROC 0.901, accuracy 86.7%), confirming that the fusion strategy transfers to real recordings, with performance decreasing as expected. Representation-level wavelet-EMD fusion provides an interpretable and transparent computational framework for analyzing non-stationary pediatric epileptiform EEG whose advantage over classical time-frequency baselines persists, at feasibility scale, on real CHB-MIT recordings and remains competitive with deep-learning baselines. Because the primary evaluation is synthetic and the external validation is a feasibility-scale demonstration, these figures should be read as evidence of methodological viability and external transportability rather than definitive clinical performance; validation on larger, multi-center and prospective pediatric cohorts is the essential next step.

papers.title: Improved Sleep and Clinical Outcomes Following a Single-Session Intervention among Adolescents with Borderline Personality Disorder Features
papers.abstract: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a serious mental illness that often emerges in adolescence. Although efficacious treatments have been developed, they are often lengthy, expensive, inaccessible, and require specialized training to deliver. Optimizing BPD prevention and early treatment is an important public health priority. Disrupted sleep is closely linked to key BPD features, and prior research has documented a range of sleep problems among BPD samples that appear to worsen symptom course and duration. This intervention trial (NCT04507308) assessed the effects of a single-session sleep-focused treatment on adolescent sleep and BPD-related symptoms. Fifty-seven adolescents (ages 13-18) with 3+ clinically impairing BPD features and at least some self-reported sleep-related difficulties participated with a caregiver. Participants completed baseline surveys, interviews, and 10-day ecological momentary assessment (EMA) protocol to examine BPD symptoms and sleep in daily life. Youth also collected at-home ambulatory electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings before undergoing the treatment informed by the Transdiagnostic Sleep and Circadian Intervention. Post-treatment, youth practiced their new sleep routine for approximately one month before undergoing reassessment (EMA, EEG, surveys). Many indices of sleep quantity and quality improved across both objective (EEG) and subjective assessments (EMA and self- and caregiver-report). Youth reported an earlier clock time at sleep onset and earlier waketime, more sleep, and fewer awakenings in daily life. Every sleep-related questionnaire score improved at post-intervention and was maintained at one-month follow-up. Multiple (though not all) indices of BPD symptoms also improved significantly. Findings suggest sleep may be a promising intervention target for at-risk youth.

papers.title: Combined vitamins C and E attenuate memory impairment and hippocampal damage in diabetic sleep-deprived mice: behavioral and molecular insights.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus (DM) and sleep disturbances are associated with cognitive impairment and hippocampal dysfunction, potentially involving oxidative stress and neuroinflammation. This study investigated the effects of vitamins C and E, individually and in combination, to determine whether their complementary antioxidant properties provide enhanced neuroprotective effects against cognitive and hippocampal alterations in diabetic sleep-deprived mice. Diabetes was induced in male BALB/c mice (25-30 g) by streptozotocin (60 mg/kg), followed by partial sleep deprivation using the inverted flowerpot method. Animals received vitamin C (50 mg/kg), vitamin E (100 mg/kg), or their combination for 20 days. Body weight and blood glucose were monitored. Spatial learning and memory were evaluated using the Morris water maze. Hippocampal histopathology, GFAP immunostaining, and expression of genes related to oxidative stress, inflammation, and neuroprotection were assessed. Vitamin E and combined vitamin C and E treatment reduced FBG and were associated with higher final body weight than untreated diabetic sleep-deprived mice. Vitamin treatments improved spatial learning and memory, with combined treatment producing greater improvements in selected behavioral outcomes. Combined treatment increased hippocampal neuronal density and reduced GFAP immunoreactivity. Vitamin treatment increased BDNF, Nrf2, and HO-1 expression and reduced iNOS, TNF-α, and IL-1β expression. Vitamin C and E, particularly in combination, were associated with improved metabolic, cognitive, and hippocampal outcomes in diabetic sleep-deprived mice, potentially involving modulation of neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress-related markers.

papers.title: Sleep Strategies and Performance Outcomes in Ultramarathon Runners: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Ultramarathon events impose prolonged physiological and cognitive demands, often spanning 1 or more nights with limited sleep opportunity. To examine associations between pre-race and intra-race sleep strategies and physical and cognitive performance outcomes in ultramarathon runners. PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science were searched from inception to July 25, 2025. Primary observational or experimental studies published in English, or available in English translation were eligible when they involved ultramarathon runners (>42.2 km) and reported sleep as a variable of interest in relation to race performance or cognitive performance. Systematic review. Level 3. Two reviewers independently extracted study design, participant characteristics, race characteristics, sleep outcomes, performance outcomes, and cognitive outcomes. Methodological quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklists. Nine studies involving 2262 participants were included, with overall low risk of bias. Of the 4 studies examining pre-race sleep, 3 reported a significant association or group difference with a race-performance outcome. Reduced sleep was generally associated with poorer physical and cognitive performance. Greater intra-race sleep duration was consistently associated with longer finish times, reflecting additional nonmoving time and increased sleep need in longer events. Greater pre-race sleep duration, including sleep extension, was associated with faster finish times, and better pre-race sleep quality was linked to higher cognitive performance. Pre-race sleep extension was associated with faster finish times, although the observational evidence does not establish causality. Further research using objective sleep measures and controlled designs is required.

papers.title: Interactions between sleep parameters and heart rate variability in temporomandibular disorders.
papers.abstract: Temporomandibular disorders (TMD) cause pain and dysfunction in the temporomandibular joints (TMJs) and masticatory muscles and significantly impact quality of life. Temporomandibular disorderrelated pain is associated with sleep disorders and affects heart rate (HR) parameters; however, data from polysomnographic studies remains inconclusive. The aim of the study was to evaluate the impact of TMD on sleep parameters recorded using video-polysomnography (vPSG) and heart rate variability (HRV) monitored with the use of a 24-hour electrocardiogram (ECG). A cross-sectional study included 93 patients with TMD diagnosed according to the Diagnostic Criteria for Temporomandibular Disorders (DC/TMD). Video-polysomnography and 24-hour ECG monitoring were conducted. Pain was assessed using the numeric rating scale (NRS) (0-10) and categorized as mild (≤5) or severe (>5). The study included 93 patients with TMD, divided into groups of low pain intensity (n = 66) and high pain intensity (n = 27). The group with high pain intensity demonstrated lower sleep efficiency (87.7% vs. 90.8%, p = 0.022) and lower oxygen saturation (94.7% vs. 95.2%, p = 0.036). Heart rate variability parameters were similar in both groups. Women reported a higher total pain score (20 vs. 10, p = 0.007) and had a higher percentage of normal-to-normal (NN) intervals differing by more than 50 ms (pNN50) (24 h: 22.5% vs. 14.2%, p = 0.013; daytime: 18.0% vs. 9.8%, p = 0.002), higher daytime root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD) (41.7 vs. 34.8, p = 0.026), and a higher nighttime HR (63.8 vs. 60.5, p = 0.047). Additionally, women demonstrated lower values for very low frequency (VLF) power (1,402.4 vs. 2,214.5, p = 0.010), low frequency (LF) power (1,415.5 vs. 2,494.5, p = 0.028), and the low frequency/high frequency (LF/HF) ratio (1.3 vs. 2.5, p < 0.001). High TMD-related pain intensity is associated with reduced sleep efficiency and lower mean oxygen saturation during sleep. Women experience higher pain intensity but lower sympathetic activation than men.

papers.title: Mental replay rescales the subjective duration of past events via alpha and theta oscillations
papers.abstract: Human memory recall is flexible in time, allowing past events to be mentally replayed at variable speeds. However, it remains unclear whether temporally rescaled replay distorts the perceived duration of remembered events, and whether such distortion is tied to changes in the retrieved content. Here we instructed participants to mentally replay previously encoded naturalistic videos at compressed, expanded, or self-paced (free) speeds while recording scalp electroencephalography (EEG). Replaying an event at an expanded pace lengthened participants' subsequent judgments of its original duration relative to free and compressed replay, and the longer an event had been replayed, the longer it was judged to have lasted. Crucially, recalled memory content was unaffected, with gist accuracy and recalled detail comparable across speed conditions. During replay, alpha and theta power were reduced under compression, and both interacted with the speed instruction in predicting reported duration. Specifically, alpha power exhibited a stronger positive relationship with duration judgments under compressed replay than under free or expanded replay. Conversely, the relationship between theta power and reported duration was significantly more positive under expanded replay than under free or compressed replay. Neural pattern similarity between instructed and later spontaneous replay varied with replay speed, yet this reinstatement neither predicted reported duration nor mediated the oscillatory effects. These findings suggest that remembered duration is not read out from the amount of content retrieved but reconstructed at retrieval through oscillatory dynamics, decoupling the subjective scaling of time from the content of memory.

papers.title: The toll of an early bell? School start time and adolescent sleep quality in Flanders, Belgium
papers.abstract: Study objectives: Adolescent sleep deprivation is a major public health concern, with insufficient and poor-quality sleep associated with adverse physical, mental and cognitive outcomes. Early school start times may contribute to sleep restriction by conflicting with the biologically delayed sleep patterns that emerge during puberty. This study examined the effect of school start times on sleep duration and sleep quality among secondary school students. Methods: Data were obtained from the 2022 Flemish Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) study, including 12,329 adolescents from grade 1 to 6 in 94 secondary schools in Flanders. School start times were obtained from participating schools and sleep duration and sleep quality were assessed using self-report measures. Data were analyzed using traditional statistical methods (i.e., linear regression) and debiased machine learning methods (i.e., assumption lean regression, dose response curves and modified treatment policies). Results: No clinically meaningful effects of school start times on sleep outcomes were observed. In machine learning models, a 10-minute delay in start time was associated with non-significant changes in sleep quality (0.01 points on a 1-5 scale; 95% CI, -0.05 to 0.06) and school-day sleep duration (3.5 minutes; 95% CI, -1.0 to 8.0). Conclusions: Within the narrow range of school start times observed in Flemish secondary schools, confidence intervals excluded clinically meaningful effects of later start times on adolescent sleep duration and sleep quality. Whether larger delays would improve sleep remains to be determined.

papers.title: Seasonal Variation in Mood and Associated Patterns of Sleep, Activity, Circadian Rhythms and Light.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms underlying seasonal mood variation are incompletely characterised. We tested whether wearable-measured sleep, activity, circadian and light exposure patterns are associated with seasonal mood variation in young Australians with emerging mood disorders. We analysed 733 observation periods from 422 participants (mean age 24.3 ± 5.5 years; 63% female) attending early-intervention clinics. Each observation included a clinical assessment paired with ≥5 valid days of wrist actigraphy. Season was modelled using sine-cosine functions of day-of-year. Sleep, activity and circadian features were reduced using joint and individual variation explained (JIVE). Light exposure features were reduced using principal component analysis (PCA) applied to light regularity, timing and exposure interval across 7 illuminance thresholds. Linear mixed-effects models tested seasonal effects on clinical outcomes; indirect associations for 12 candidate JIVE/PCA variables were estimated by cluster bootstrap. Depressive symptoms (β = -0.67, P = .023) and negative symptoms (β = -0.17, P = .041) peaked in winter, whereas manic symptoms peaked in autumn (β = 0.24, P = .019). Winter increases in negative symptoms were associated with an 'extended sleep with phase-delayed activity' profile (indirect β = -0.015, P < .002) and a 'constrained pattern of moderate-to-bright indoor light exposure' profile (indirect β = -0.038, P = .002), reflecting high day-to-day consistency with a narrow daily exposure window. The light association persisted after adjustment for time spent above the light threshold, which itself was not associated with symptoms. Winter increases in depressive symptoms were associated with lower overall physical activity levels (indirect β = -0.009, P = .040). No indirect associations were identified for manic symptoms. In this transdiagnostic youth sample, seasonal variation in mood was modest but was accompanied by differences in how personal light exposure was arranged across the day, not only in how much light was received and in daily activity patterns. These cross-sectional associations identify light patterning and activity rhythms as candidate modifiable targets for prospective and interventional research.

papers.title: Gene-by-Sleep Duration Interaction for Glycemic Traits in More Than 480,000 Individuals.
papers.abstract: The biological mechanisms of how sleep duration impacts type 2 diabetes pathogenesis and glycemic control are unclear. This study reveals 16 loci (11 novel) that interact with either short or long sleep duration to influence hemoglobin A1c, fasting glucose, or fasting insulin. Short and long sleep duration loci were nonoverlapping. Regulation of copper and diacylglycerol levels appear as distinct cellular mechanisms implicated by long and short sleep duration loci, respectively. Identified gene targets present insight for potential type 2 diabetes therapeutic design approaches related to JIP1-c-Jun N-terminal kinase interaction disruption, pericyte health, N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor activity, anti-inflammatory and leptin-enhancing dietary supplements, and serpins.

papers.title: Federated Spiking GANs with Rényi Differential Privacy for privacy-preserving synthetic EEG generation in brain-computer interfaces.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) data used in brain-computer and brain-machine interfaces (BCI/BMI) contain sensitive, user-specific information, creating privacy risks in consumer applications such as gaming, human augmentation, and virtual reality. Existing methods like encryption and anonymization either fail to protect data during analysis or still expose identifiable attributes. While differential privacy (DP) offers formal protection, it often reduces data utility. The key challenge is to generate synthetic EEG data that protects sensitive attributes while retaining temporal features for downstream use. To address this, we developed a federated spiking generative framework that integrates a spiking neural network (SNN)-based generator, temporally correlated noise, an artificial neural network (ANN)-based discriminator, and Rényi differential privacy (RDP) within a federated learning framework. The SNN-based generator captures temporal characteristics, and the ANN-based discriminator maintains classification accuracy. Federated training prevents centralization of raw client data, while privacy is preserved through controlled perturbation of spike-train and membrane-potential representations, supported by RDP-based privacy accounting. We evaluated our architecture against methods such as RDP-TimeGAN, RDP-CRNN-GAN, RDP-RCGAN, and RDP-Clare-GAN, demonstrating that our approach preserves temporal features and downstream utility while maintaining privacy in synthetic EEG generation. This solution enables privacy-preserving generation of distributed synthetic EEG data for BCI/BMI research and development.

papers.title: EEG-Based Cognitive Overload-Driven Adaptive Training for Enhancing Performance Under Simulated High-Stress Space Operation Tasks.
papers.abstract: Given the potential for highly complex and high-risk space operation tasks to induce cognitive overload in operators, effective training is crucial for maintaining mission performance and safety. Conventional adaptive training often struggles to balance task challenge while preventing overload. To address this limitation, this study proposes an EEG-based cognitive overload-driven adaptive training method that integrates hybrid feature selection, Normalized Fast Dynamic Time Warping (NFDTW)-based feature alignment and a shared knowledge layer to improve online cognitive overload detection under nonstationary conditions. A dual-factor task regulation strategy combining task performance and cognitive overload states is further developed to adjust task difficulty based on these two factors. The results showed that the proposed detection method achieved online detection accuracies of 92.07% and 84.67% on the two datasets, respectively, with maximum relative improvements of 7.74% and 8.34% over the comparison methods. The adaptive training strategy was further evaluated in a VR-based robotic arm docking task involving three groups: fixed, control, and adaptive. Mixed-design ANOVA showed that the adaptive group exhibited significant improvements in task performance and SAS as well as more favorable changes in EEG features. Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc comparisons further revealed significant group differences ([Formula: see text]). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of EEG-based cognitive overload-driven adaptive training for complex space operation scenarios.

papers.title: Who's Been Sleeping in My Bedroom? Associations Between Co-Sleeping with Dogs, Cats, or Children and Sleep and Cardiorespiratory Physiology Among WHOOP Users.
papers.abstract: Co-sleeping with pets or children is common, yet its associations with sleep, cardiorespiratory physiology, and behavioral outcomes are understudied. We examined within-person associations between co-sleeping with a dog, cat, or child and sleep characteristics, measures of cardiorespiratory physiology, and next-day physical activity. We analyzed 1,649,083 person-days from 11,733 adults wearing the WHOOP wearable device. Participants self-reported nightly co-sleeping via a daily journal in the device's companion smartphone application. Linear mixed-effects models compared nights with and without co-sleeping within the same individual. Co-sleeping was associated with lower resting heart rate (0.8-1.1 beats/min), lower respiratory rate (0.04-0.07 breaths/min), and higher heart rate variability (1.41-1.95 ms). Sleep outcomes were mixed, with longer sleep duration (5.5-9.6 min) but more disturbances (0.36-0.40 instances) and slightly less restorative sleep (0.23-1.17%). Associations were generally consistent across groups, although child co-sleeping was associated with greater sleep disruption. Next-day physical activity was higher following dog and cat co-sleeping (7.6 and 7.4 intensity-weighted min, respectively) but lower following child co-sleeping (-2.6 intensity-weighted min). Despite statistical significance, all standardized effect sizes were small (β range: 0.008-0.045). Co-sleeping was associated with small differences in cardiorespiratory physiology (lower resting heart rate, higher heart rate variability) alongside mildly greater sleep disruption. The small magnitude of these associations suggests that co-sleeping decisions may be influenced more by personal and contextual factors than by expectations of substantive physiologic or sleep-related impacts.

papers.title: Subtle Alterations of Tidal Breathing Variables in Healthy Late Preterm Neonates at Term-Equivalent Age.
papers.abstract: Late-preterm birth is associated with increased respiratory morbidity, but tidal breathing at term-equivalent age remains incompletely characterized. We hypothesized that healthy late-preterm neonates would differ from term neonates, with the between-group difference in tPTEF/tE designated as the primary outcome. In this prospective cross-sectional study, 60 healthy late-preterm and 60 term neonates underwent tidal breathing analysis (MasterScreen PAED) at term-equivalent age (40 weeks' postmenstrual age) during natural quiet sleep without sedation. Late-preterm neonates had lower tPTEF/tE (27.4 ± 7.0% vs. 31.2 ± 6.9%; Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted p = 0.028; Cohen's d = 0.544) and VPTEF/VE [28.6 (25.1-31.0)% vs. 32.1 (27.3-35.5)%; adjusted p = 0.028; Cliff's δ = 0.304] than term neonates. Respiratory rate was higher (53.2 ± 9.1 vs. 49.6 ± 9.5 breaths/min), but not significant after correction (adjusted p = 0.126). No other tidal breathing variables differed significantly after correction. In the primary multivariable model, each additional week of exact gestational age was associated with a 1.18-percentage-point increase in tPTEF/tE after adjustment for sex, body weight, and crown-heel length (B = 1.182; 95% CI, 0.540-1.823; β = 0.323; p < 0.001). When postnatal age replaced gestational age, the association was inverse (B = -0.167/day; 95% CI, -0.263 to -0.071; β = -0.306; p < 0.001). At term-equivalent age, healthy late-preterm neonates had modestly lower tPTFEF/tE and VPTEF/VE than term neonates. These findings may reflect subtle maturational differences in expiratory flow dynamics associated with late-preterm birth.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture improves endometrial receptivity and pregnancy outcomes in controlled ovarian hyperstimulation rats by restoring Per2 circadian rhythm.
papers.abstract: Controlled ovarian hyperstimulation (COH) is a critical step in in vitro fertilization-embryo transfer (IVF-ET). However, the decline in endometrial receptivity caused by COH severely restricts the success rate of implantation. Previous studies mostly focused on static molecular events, lacking a systematic exploration from the perspective of dynamic rhythms. This study aims to explore whether electroacupuncture (EA) can improve endometrial receptivity and pregnancy outcomes by repairing the disordered rhythm of the core clock gene Per2 in the endometrium caused by COH from the perspective of chronobiology. A COH model was established using 126 Sprague - Dawley (SD) rats. Following EA intervention, dynamic sampling was conducted during the implantation window to assess clock gene rhythmicity, the expression of receptivity - related factors, and uterine morphological changes. Per2-/- mice were used to preliminarily investigate whether Per2 participates in mediating the effects of EA. COH induced an abnormal increase in serum progesterone, leading to desynchronization of the endometrial clock gene network. Among them, the peak delay of the core clock gene Per2 was highly coupled with the abnormal peak of progesterone in time, and presented an anti - phase oscillatory pattern with the expression of the angiogenesis factor Vegf. During the implantation window, the expression of Vegf and integrin αvβ3 was down - regulated, the development of pinopodes degenerated, and the pregnancy rate was significantly reduced. EA could correct the abnormal progesterone level, repair the rhythm parameters of Per2, up - regulate the expression of Vegf and integrin αvβ3, improve the development of pinopodes, and significantly increase the pregnancy rate. In Per2-/- mice, the up - regulating effect of EA on Vegf and Integrin αvβ3 was significantly weakened, preliminarily suggesting that Per2 may participate in mediating the effects of EA on endometrial receptivity. This study provided preliminary evidence for a novel mechanism by which COH impairs endometrial receptivity from the perspective of dynamic circadian rhythm, providing experimental evidence for EA as an adjuvant intervention strategy based on circadian clock regulation in IVF-ET cycles.

papers.title: The moderating role of anger rumination and self-control in the day-to-day associations between irritability and sleep in male adolescents: An exploratory experience sampling method study.
papers.abstract: Irritability is highly prevalent in adolescents and may be exacerbated by sleep disturbances, with sleep patterns undergoing significant changes during this developmental period. Reciprocally, poor sleep may generate an increase in anger dysregulation. This exploratory study investigates the day-to-day associations between sleep and irritability, as well as the moderating effects of maladaptive (i.e., anger rumination) and adaptive (i.e., self-control) emotion regulation (ER) strategies. Fifty-six male adolescents aged 12-18, with diverse sleep and emotional problems, participated in a 9-day experience sampling method study. Participants also completed self-report questionnaires assessing irritability, sleep quantity and quality, and maladaptive and adaptive ER strategies. Linear mixed effect models with lagged covariates were used to test associations and moderating effects. At the within-person level, sleep quality was associated with next-day irritability (βstd = -0.92, 95% CI [-1.31, -0.53). Higher daily anger rumination (βstd = 0.25, 95% CI [0.17, 0.34]), and daily self-control (βstd = -0.18, 95% CI [-0.27, -0.10]) were directly associated with higher next-day irritability. At the between-person level, lower self-control was also associated with higher next-day irritability (βstd = -0.52, 95% CI [-0.77, -0.27]). Interactions between daily sleep quality and between-person anger rumination ( β std interaction = 0.18, 95% [0.07, 0.30]), and self-control ( β std interaction = 0.75, 95% CI [0.38, 1.12]) were related with irritability. Reciprocally, lower irritability from the day was associated with better sleep quality the following night (βstd = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.20, -0.01]). These preliminary findings suggest that sleep may be related to next-day irritability in adolescent boys and may vary as a function of anger rumination and self-control. Additionally, irritability also showed a potential association with subsequent sleep. However, findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small, all-male adolescent sample. Future studies including larger and more diverse adolescent samples are needed to assess their generalizability and robustness.

papers.title: Association Between Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorder and Noninfectious Uveitis: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: Circadian misalignment influences ocular immune homeostasis, inflammatory signaling, and blood-retinal barrier integrity, each implicated in the pathogenesis of noninfectious uveitis (NIU). Whether clinically diagnosed circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder (CRSD) is associated with incident NIU is unknown. This study examined that association in a large multicenter cohort. This retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX federated network. Adults with CRSD (ICD-10 G47.2) were compared with adults who underwent polysomnography without a sleep disorder. Patients with uveitis before the index date or with causes of infectious or secondary intraocular inflammation were excluded. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression estimated adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) for incident anterior and composite NIU, adjusting for demographics, systemic comorbidities, corticosteroid exposure, and prior ophthalmology encounters. Major depressive disorder and appendicitis served as positive and negative control outcomes. The CRSD cohort included 47 323 adults and the comparator cohort 22 241 adults. CRSD was independently associated with an increased hazard of incident anterior NIU (aHR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.11-2.61) and composite NIU (aHR, 1.84; 95% CI, 1.21-2.79). Control outcomes performed as expected, with a strong association for major depressive disorder (aHR, 2.19; 95% CI, 2.10-2.29) and no association for appendicitis (aHR, 1.12; 95% CI, 0.87-1.45). Clinically diagnosed CRSD was independently associated with an increased risk of incident NIU. These findings support a potential role for circadian dysregulation in ocular inflammatory disease and warrant prospective confirmation.

papers.title: Circadian clock adjusted classes improve sleep, circadian health, and academic performance in medical freshmen.

This study evaluated whether a later-start schedule improves academic outcomes and circadian rhythms in first-year medical students. Incoming students (n = 220) completed the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire; those with high social jetlag (SJL >120 min, n = 71) were randomized into either a later-start schedule (LS; classes ≥10:00 a.m., n = 30) or a standard early-start schedule (ES; 8:00 a.m., n = 41). Actigraphy data were collected from 112 students prior to examinations. Based on the objective temperature circadian phase (TCP) with a median acrophase split at 3:59 a.m. ES participants were categorized asearly (ETCP-ES, n = 41) or late (LTCP-ES, n = 41). All LS participants exhibited a TCP later than 3:59 a.m. and remained LTCP-LS group (n = 30). Associations between scheduling, circadian metrics, and exam scores were analyzed using regression and sex-adjusted ANCOVA. TCP predicted exam scores overall (β = -0.217, p = 0.021), most evidently within ES (β = -0.291, p = 0.008). LTCP-ES students scored lower than ETCP-ES students (p = 0.025). LTCP-LS students performed similarly to ETCP-ES students and showed greater circadian robustness, including higher rest-activity stability (p = 0.031), greater blue-light stability (p = 0.029), and longer sleep duration (p = 0.013).

papers.title: Assessment of the duration of continuous EEG monitoring in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) can detect seizures and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI) in patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). Because a standard duration of continuous EEG monitoring to capture these complications has not been established in aSAH, we compared a standard 6- or 7-day cEEG monitoring protocol versus longer periods of monitoring. We performed a retrospective analysis of aSAH patients ≥18 years old grouped by standard monitoring protocol (6-7 days, group 1) and those with longer monitoring (>7 days, group 2). Clinical characteristics, EEG features, length of stay (LOS) and functional outcome were compared using univariate analyses. Multivariable analyses tested the association between the groups and vasospasm, DCI, LOS, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). 19 patients met criteria for group 1 and 16 patients for group 2. We found no difference in EEG's detection of worsening abnormal EEG activity, vasospasm and DCI. ICU and hospital LOS in group 2 were nearly double that of group 1 (ICU: 25.5 (19.5-35) vs. 14 (11-21) days, p = 0.0003; hospital: 32.5 (29.5-48) vs. 18 (13-29) days, p = 0.003). Good outcome (mRS ≤2) at discharge and at 6 months was similar in both groups (21.1% vs. 0% and 56.3% vs. 46.2%). In multivariable analysis, EEG duration was independently associated with ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and mRS at 6 months. Longer EEG monitoring correlated with significantly longer ICU and hospital LOS but not with vasospasm, DCI, and functional outcome at 6 months. Larger studies to confirm our findings are warranted.

papers.title: Indoor NO2, temperature, and humidity in relation to maternal stress, sleep, and cognitive performance during pregnancy.
papers.abstract: Evidence characterising indoor environmental exposures and their effects on maternal neurobehavioural well-being during pregnancy remains scarce. papers.title: Resting-state EEG functional connectivity changes following memantine administration in children with autism spectrum disorder: an exploratory pre-post study.
papers.abstract: Despite the widespread use of memantine in modulating excitatory/inhibitory balance, the precise changes in the topology of brain networks following memantine administration in preschool children remain clearly undefined. Resting-state electroencephalogram (EEG) signals were recorded before and after the intervention. functional connectivity matrices were extracted using the Phase Locking Value (PLV) index. SPN analysis identified distinct spatial components of network reorganization: (1) localized connectivity suppression in the fronto-central (Fz, F3) and left occipital (O1) regions captured by lower-order spatial filters, and (2) reinforcement of long-range functional coupling and enhanced nodal centrality in the right parietal (P4) and left temporal (T3) regions in higher-order filters. papers.title: Network analysis of frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction in older patients: a cross-sectional study stratified by chronic disease burden.
papers.abstract: Multimorbidity and chronic disease burden are common among older patients and are closely associated with frailty, poor sleep, and reduced subjective well-being. However, total-score-based analyses may obscure item-level interactions across health domains. This study examined the network structure of frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction in older patients and explored whether association patterns varied across chronic disease burden levels. This cross-sectional study included 1,107 older patients. Multimorbidity was defined as the presence of two or more chronic diseases. Frailty, sleep quality, and life satisfaction were assessed using the Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illnesses, and Loss of Weight (FRAIL) scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), respectively. A regularized partial correlation network was estimated using the graphical least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) with extended Bayesian information criterion (EBIC) model selection (EBICglasso), with scale items or components as nodes. Strength, expected influence, and bridge centrality were calculated. Stratified analyses were conducted by number of chronic diseases, and bootstrap procedures were used to assess network accuracy and stability. Multimorbidity was present in 1,078 participants (97.4%), and the median number of chronic diseases was 5 (IQR, 3-6). Network analysis showed that SWLS-related nodes had relatively high strength and bridge strength, indicating relatively high statistical connectivity within the overall network and across communities. Sleep-related nodes, particularly sleep latency, use of sleeping medication, and daytime dysfunction, were prominent in signed centrality indices. Frailty nodes were mainly connected to SWLS nodes through negative edges. The SWLS community showed dense internal connections, whereas frailty and sleep quality were linked to life satisfaction primarily through negative cross-community edges. In descriptive stratified analyses, negative cross-community connections appeared more pronounced in the group with ≥ 5 chronic diseases. Because the cutoff was data-driven and no formal network comparison test was performed, the apparent between-group differences should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than statistically confirmed. Network stability analyses indicated acceptable stability. Among older patients, life satisfaction-related nodes showed relatively high overall connectivity, while several sleep-related nodes showed notable statistical associations within the estimated network. Given the high prevalence of multimorbidity in this sample, multidisciplinary assessment and health management should consider the interrelations among sleep problems, frailty, and life satisfaction in the context of chronic disease burden. Network analysis may provide exploratory evidence on cross-domain associations in complex health problems among older patients, but apparent differences across chronic disease burden groups require confirmation using formal network comparison tests and longitudinal designs.

papers.title: Case Report: Smith-Magenis syndrome with bilateral high-grade vesicoureteral reflux, hypothyroidism, and seizure in infancy.
papers.abstract: Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS) is a rare neurodevelopmental and multisystem disorder caused mainly by 17p11.2 deletions involving RAI1. Because the characteristic behavioral and sleep phenotype may not yet be apparent, diagnosis in infancy can be challenging. We report a 9-month-old boy with recurrent febrile urinary tract infection, bilateral hydronephrosis with ureteral dilatation, hypothyroidism, global developmental delay, hypotonia, brachydactyly, dysmorphic features, phimosis, and short penis. Voiding cystourethrography demonstrated bilateral grade IV vesicoureteral reflux (VUR). Renal scintigraphy showed focal right renal cortical defects; DTPA effective renal plasma flow was 180.33 mL/min in the left kidney and 133.77 mL/min in the right kidney, corresponding to split function of 57.4% and 42.6%. Trio whole-exome sequencing with copy-number-variant analysis identified a de novo 3.63-Mb deletion at 17p11.2 encompassing RAI1, confirming SMS; a maternally inherited heterozygous DUOX2 likely pathogenic variant was also detected, but its contribution to hypothyroidism remains unproven. Infection improved with antibiotics, levothyroxine was resumed, and amoxicillin/clavulanate prophylaxis was initiated. Surgery for phimosis was postponed after an afebrile sleep-related seizure. Follow-up showed improved renal indices, no recurrent urinary tract infection, normalized thyroid function, and no definite abnormality on video-electroencephalography, although developmental delay persisted and brief seizure-like ocular events remained under evaluation. This case shows that high-grade bilateral VUR with recurrent infection and a syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype can be an early presentation of SMS and warrants copy-number analysis, renal protection, and coordinated endocrine, neurologic, developmental, and urologic follow-up.

papers.title: When a Seizure Reveals More Than a Hemorrhage: When to Suspect Cerebral Cavernous Malformations.
papers.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are low-flow vascular malformations that may be asymptomatic or present with seizures, hemorrhage, headache, or focal neurological deficits. Most are sporadic and solitary, whereas familial CCMs are associated with multiple lesions and autosomal-dominant inheritance. Distinguishing between these forms is clinically relevant for long-term management. We present a 33-year-old woman who presented with generalized tonic-clonic seizures following sleep deprivation. Computed tomography (CT) initially suggested a left frontal intraparenchymal hemorrhage. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) subsequently revealed two left frontal Zabramski type II CCMs. Electroencephalography showed cortical dysfunction with paroxysmal activity and contralateral propagation. Antiseizure treatment with phenytoin was initiated and later supplemented with levetiracetam. The patient remained asymptomatic and was referred for tertiary evaluation. This case highlights the diagnostic limitations of CT and the importance of MRI for CCM characterization and detection of multiple lesions. The presence of two cavernomas and a potentially relevant family history raises suspicion for familial CCM, although these findings alone do not establish a hereditary diagnosis. Genetic evaluation and detailed family assessment should therefore be considered. Treatment should be individualized; conservative management is appropriate in selected stable patients, whereas microsurgery and stereotactic radiosurgery are reserved for specific clinical scenarios.

papers.title: The role and mechanism of endothelial cell-specific molecule-1 in respiratory diseases.
papers.abstract: Endothelial cell-specific molecule-1 (ESM1) is a soluble dermatan sulfate proteoglycan and is mainly expressed in pulmonary endothelial cells. It is reported that ESM1 plays an important role in promoting cell proliferation, such as metabolic reprogramming, and inhibiting autophagy. In addition, ESM1 exerts a dual regulatory effect on inflammation. However, the mechanism of the dual regulatory effect of ESM1 on inflammation remains unclear. Moreover, evidence suggests that ESM1 is involved in multiple signaling pathways, such as the EGFR/ESM1, EGFR/HER3-Akt/ANGPT2, HGF/c-MET, VEGF-A/ESM1, mTOR, and ZEB1/PI3K/AKT pathways. Increasing studies suggested that ESM1 is involved in various respiratory diseases, such as lung cancer, obstructive sleep apnea hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS), pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and acute lung injury (ALI)/acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). In lung cancer, ESM1 promotes cancer cell proliferation through the EGFR, NF-κB, and HGF/c-MET signaling pathways. In OSAHS, ESM1 enhances inflammatory factor secretion and monocyte-endothelial cell adhesion through the HIF-1α/VEGF signaling pathway. In PAH, ESM1 may promote vascular remodeling and inflammation via a positive feedback loop with TNF-α. Conversely, in ALI/ARDS, ESM1 may inhibit leukocyte recruitment to reduce inflammation. However, the specific roles and mechanisms of ESM1 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, and pneumonia need to be further explored. Accordingly, ESM1 may serve as a potential therapeutic target for various respiratory diseases.

papers.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes with High-Volume Hemodiafiltration Versus High-Flux Hemodialysis Across Clinical Subgroups: Results from the CONVINCE Trial.
papers.abstract: High-volume hemodiafiltration (HDF) improves survival and attenuates decline in selected patient-reported outcome (PRO) domains versus high-flux hemodialysis (HD). Whether benefits differ across clinically relevant subgroups remains uncertain. We conducted a prespecified subgroup analysis of the multicenter CONVINCE randomized controlled trial comparing high-volume post-dilution HDF (≥23 L/session) with high-flux HD in adults receiving maintenance dialysis. Eight PROMIS domains were assessed quarterly over a median follow-up of 30 months. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated longitudinal PRO changes and treatment-by-subgroup interactions by prespecified baseline characteristics: age, sex, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, dialysis vintage, vascular access type, and residual urine volume. Joint-model sensitivity analyses of all eight longitudinal PROMIS trajectories and time to death assessed informative dropout due to death. Of 1360 randomized participants, 1211 with baseline and follow-up PRO assessments were included. PRO treatment effects were broadly consistent across prespecified clinical subgroups, without evidence of clinically meaningful heterogeneity. Models adjusted for baseline sociodemographic and clinical characteristics showed nominal treatment-by-subgroup interactions for dialysis vintage and physical function (P = 0.03), age and pain interference (P = 0.02), and dialysis vintage and sleep disturbance (P = 0.04). Joint-model sensitivity analyses accounting for informative dropout due to mortality reproduced the first two interactions and identified nominal interactions for vascular access type and sleep disturbance (P = 0.03) and cardiovascular disease status and cognitive function (P = 0.05). Nominal interactions were unadjusted for multiple comparisons and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Findings should not guide selection or exclusion of patients for high-volume HDF based on patient-reported outcomes.

papers.title: A systematic review of economic evaluations of strategies to diagnose obstructive sleep apnoea in adults.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a chronic condition characterised by recurrent episodes of apnoea and hypopnoea. People with untreated OSA are at increased risk of excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS), functional impairment and developing cardiovascular conditions, metabolic and neurocognitive diseases. EDS is a key determinant of quality of life (QoL) and is associated with increased healthcare utilisation and accident risk. Untreated OSA can also lead to impaired work productivity, reduced health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and life expectancy, which contribute to the UK economic burden. To review and critically appraise all published economic evaluations that assessed the cost-effectiveness of devices and strategies to diagnose and manage people with moderate-to-severe OSA. This systematic review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews guidelines and registered in the Prospective Register of Ongoing Systematic Reviews (CRD42024535732). We searched electronic databases up to March 2025. Two reviewers undertook screening, data extraction and quality appraisal using recognised reporting quality and methodological quality appraisal tools. The findings were summarised and discussed narratively. Twenty-nine studies were included. Fifteen studies included an economic evaluation alongside a clinical trial and 14 studies were model-based economic analyses. Although many analyses were methodologically sound in their overall approach, there were concerns regarding choice of time horizon, selection of health states, undertaking pre-model analyses and long-term adherence and efficacy of continuous positive airway pressure treatment (CPAP). Substantial methodological heterogeneity was identified across studies, including variation in diagnostic thresholds and scoring criteria used, model structures and assumptions regarding treatment adherence. Only four of twenty-nine included studies used home respiratory polygraphy (HRP) as a comparator, limiting the direct applicability of much of the evidence to the UK setting. Past economic analyses offer insight into the methods used to assess the cost-effectiveness of strategies to diagnose OSA. These economic analyses are a useful framework to build on, but clear gaps exist in the clinical and economic evidence. Future economic evaluations should prioritise contemporary diagnostic pathways and technologies, use consistent diagnostic definitions, and incorporate more realistic modelling of long-term treatment adherence and benefit. Until such information becomes available, the true cost-effectiveness of these strategies remains unknown.

papers.title: "It Just Puts You Out!" Tranq Sleep, Sensory Discernment, and the Experience of Consuming Xylazine-Adulterated Fentanyl in Rural North Carolina

Data were analyzed using a combined deductive-inductive thematic approach in QSR NVivo 14.0. While nearly all participants expressed strong aversion to xylazine, a meaningful minority valued its amplifying effects to improve a diminishing fentanyl high. Findings extend the xylazine literature geographically and pharmacologically and underscore the urgency of harm reduction responses tailored to the distinctive harms of xylazine. In particular, adverse health outcomes that accumulate during episodes of protracted and unarousable sedation, including physical injury, victimization, and the severe withdrawal syndrome that follows upon awakening.

papers.title: The impact of menstruation-related symptoms on women's quality of life, work productivity, and economic burden: a structured narrative review.
papers.abstract: Menstruation-related disorders, including dysmenorrhoea, premenstrual syndrome (PMS)/ premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), and heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB)/ abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB), are common among women of reproductive age and associated with impairments in quality of life (QOL), mental health, and daily functioning. Increasing evidence indicates that these conditions adversely affect academic and work productivity, with presenteeism constituting a major component of the economic burden. However, the existing evidence remains fragmented. We conducted a structured narrative review supported by a targeted literature search of PubMed and Scopus. Studies published in English between January 2014 and December 2025 were considered if they included female individuals aged 14-59 years and examined menstruation-related symptoms in relation to QOL, work productivity, academic or occupational functioning, or economic outcomes. Because of heterogeneity in study designs, populations, and outcome measures, findings were synthesised thematically rather than quantitatively pooled. A total of 86 studies were used to inform the thematic synthesis. Across conditions, menstruation-related disorders were consistently associated with reduced health-related QOL, psychological distress, and impaired academic and occupational functioning. Productivity loss was observed across disorders and predominantly driven by presenteeism rather than by absenteeism. Dysmenorrhoea and PMS/PMDD were associated with both absenteeism and presenteeism, whereas HMB/AUB was strongly associated with work impairment, which is frequently mediated by anaemia-related symptoms. Psychological distress, including anxiety, depressive symptoms, emotional dysregulation, and sleep disturbance, has emerged as a key contributor to QOL impairment across age groups and regions. Lifestyle factors appeared to modify symptom severity and functional impact. Although treatment and medical consultations often improved symptoms, productivity gains were inconsistent. This review highlights the multidimensional burden of menstruation-related disorders extending from physical symptoms to mental health and functional outcomes. The predominance of presenteeism suggested that conventional metrics based on absenteeism underestimate the true societal impact. The observed gap between symptom improvement and functional recovery underscored the need for integrated approaches that could address both clinical and psychosocial pathways.
